name: Sun-proof masks and capes for freckle avoidance

image.caption: Sun-proof masks and capes for freckle avoidance

lead: In the early 1900s freckles were widely seen as something to avoid, and covering up was the obvious prevention. Veils, masks, capes and similar coverings were worn outdoors so sunlight did not reach the face and skin.

By then it was generally accepted that freckles were produced by sunlight acting on the skin, and period authors wrote about which veil colours blocked more light. Modern sun protection works on the same principle that physical coverage reduces exposure.

paras: A veil, mask or cape was worn when out in the sun, often together with a hat, parasol or gloves. Commentators of the time favoured reddish-brown or gauze veils over blue or white ones.
Period sources warned that veils could tire the eyes, and the freckle-removal creams that went with the era often contained mercury compounds.

chain: Veil, mask or cape blocks sunlight
Skin is not stimulated to freckle or tan
angle.text: Women wore coverings outdoors so sunlight did not reach the face, on the understanding that sun exposure produces freckles. Staying covered or in shade was how freckles that had already appeared were also said to fade.

lead: Before modern sunscreens, avoiding freckles meant keeping the sun off the skin. Writers in the early 1900s treated covering up as the obvious method, and veils were the main protective measure they discussed [1]. Masks and capes belong to the same family of coverings.

Ideas about colour mattered. Fletcher (1901) judged blue and white veils to give no protection because sunlight passed through them, preferred reddish-brown veils, and recommended gauze or chiffon, while warning that veils were hard on the eyes [1]. Ayer (1902) noted summer freckles faded when a person stayed indoors or in shade [1].

These coverings sat alongside a large freckle-removal market, with mass-made creams from the late nineteenth century such as Dr. Berry's Freckle Ointment, Othine and Stillman's [2]. Pale smooth skin was the Western ideal and freckles carried class associations [2].

paras: Pale, smooth skin was the Western beauty ideal from the medieval period into the twentieth century, and freckles marked outdoor laborers, so rejecting them reflected class and other biases [2]. In 1845 Dr. William Kittoe advised women never to go into the sun uncovered and to use a large bonnet, veil or parasol [2].

Early-1900s writers debated veil colour: Fletcher (1901) said blue and white veils offered no protection and favoured reddish-brown, and noted that red veils and gloves were unattractive [1]. Gauze or chiffon were recommended when protection was needed [1].

Home remedies used weak acids or mild bleaches such as lactic acid, lemon juice, vinegar, sour milk and borax [1]. Commercial creams often contained mercury compounds, and a 1914 author described mercury as dangerous while still calling it the surest remover [1]. After the 1938 US Food, Drugs and Cosmetics Act the FDA pushed mercury levels to 5% or less, and such creams stayed on sale until the 1970s [1].
